items.followUp: Define boiling point and state how intermolecular forces affect it.

rubric.why: Identifies the vapour above a liquid in a closed vessel.
rubric.description: States that vapour pressure is exerted by vapour above its liquid in a closed vessel.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying vapour above a liquid in a closed vessel.

rubric.why: Includes the pressure and the equilibrium condition that characterise vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Explains that this pressure occurs when evaporation and condensation are in equilibrium at a given temperature.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the pressure at equilibrium, preferably specifying evaporation and condensation.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure is the pressure exerted by the vapour of a liquid above its surface in a closed vessel.
At a given temperature, it is measured when evaporation and condensation are in equilibrium.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature affects the rate of evaporation.

rubric.why: States the effect of stronger intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces reduce the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking stronger forces with lower evaporation.

rubric.why: States the corresponding effect of weaker intermolecular attraction.
rubric.description: Weaker intermolecular forces increase the rate of evaporation.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking weaker forces with higher or faster evaporation.

modelAnswer: When intermolecular forces are strong, more energy is needed for molecules to escape from the liquid, so evaporation is slower.
When intermolecular forces are weak, molecules escape more easily, so evaporation is faster.

items.followUp: What is a saturated solution? Give one example.

rubric.why: Gives the defining nature of a solution.
rubric.description: Defines a solution as a homogeneous (uniform) mixture.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a solution is a homogeneous or uniform mixture.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of a solution.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as salt dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one correct example.

modelAnswer: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
Salt dissolved in water is an example of a solution.

items.followUp: Name two factors that affect the rate of dissolving a solid in a liquid.

rubric.why: Recognises one accepted factor affecting solubility.
rubric.description: Names one factor that affects solubility, such as temperature, pressure, or the nature of the solute and solvent.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid factor.

rubric.description: Names a second factor affecting solubility.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a second valid factor distinct from the first.

items.followUp: Why is aluminium also used for making electrical wires?

rubric.why: Identifies copper's ability to conduct electricity.
rubric.description: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that copper conducts electricity well.

rubric.why: Identifies the property that lets copper be shaped into wires.
rubric.description: Copper is ductile and can be drawn into thin wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that copper is ductile or can be drawn into wires.

modelAnswer: Copper is an excellent conductor of electricity.
It is ductile, so it can be drawn into thin wires.

items.followUp: Why does oxygen usually have a valency of two?

rubric.why: Identifies the number of electrons in chlorine's outermost shell.
rubric.description: Chlorine has seven electrons in its outermost shell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that chlorine has seven valence electrons.

rubric.why: Explains that chlorine needs one electron to complete its outer shell.
rubric.description: Chlorine gains or shares one electron to attain a stable outer shell, so its valency is one.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the one-electron requirement or the resulting valency of one.

modelAnswer: A chlorine atom has seven electrons in its outermost shell.
It needs one more electron to complete that shell; therefore, its valency is one.

items.followUp: Why is the second ionization energy of sodium greater than its first ionization energy?

rubric.why: Describes removal of the first electron from magnesium.
rubric.description: The first ionization energy removes one outer 3s electron from a neutral Mg atom to form Mg⁺.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the first electron removed and the Mg⁺ product.

rubric.why: States the comparison and reflects the stronger attraction after the first electron is removed.
rubric.description: The second ionization energy is greater than the first because the remaining electron is attracted more strongly by the positively charged Mg⁺ ion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the second ionization energy is higher and giving the increased attraction as the reason.

modelAnswer: The first ionization energy removes one outer 3s electron from Mg to form Mg⁺.
The second ionization energy removes an electron from Mg⁺ and is greater than the first because the remaining electrons are held more strongly by the positive ion.

items.followUp: Write the chemical formula for aluminium oxide using the valencies of aluminium and oxygen.

rubric.why: Begins formula writing with the symbols of the elements or ions.
rubric.description: Write the symbols of the elements or ions in the compound.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct symbols, such as Mg and Cl in the example.

rubric.why: Uses valencies to determine the subscripts in the formula.
rubric.description: Write the valency of each element or ion below its symbol.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly stating or showing the valencies.

rubric.why: Shows the standard method for transferring valencies to subscripts.
rubric.description: Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing or applying the criss-cross method.

rubric.why: Ensures the subscripts are reduced to the simplest whole-number ratio.
rubric.description: Reduce the subscripts by any common factor, if possible.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for simplifying subscripts when required.

rubric.why: Demonstrates a correct resulting formula or the required bracket rule for polyatomic ions.
rubric.description: Write the final formula correctly; use brackets around a polyatomic ion when more than one is needed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example formula or the correct bracket rule.

modelAnswer: Write the symbols of the elements or ions; for example, Mg and Cl.
Write their valencies: Mg = 2 and Cl = 1.
Interchange the valencies and write them as subscripts: Mg₁Cl₂.
Remove the subscript 1 to obtain MgCl₂.
If a polyatomic ion occurs more than once, put it in brackets before writing its subscript.
